title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Look up green in the red cabbage color chart in 12.1: is it an acid color or a base color? Then use BRA for litmus and "pink means base" for phenolphthalein.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Build the salt from the ion charges, then balance Cl and H. The gas tells you what you would see.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Acid + base → salt + water. Ca<sup>2+</sup> needs two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, so count the HNO<sub>3</sub> and waters that takes; the salt is the base's cation with the acid's anion.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use BAD: the reactant that loses an H from left to right is the acid; the one that gains an H is the base. Each partner on the right shares a common piece with it.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: To make a conjugate acid, add one H<sup>+</sup>: one more H, and the charge goes up by 1.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: does water gain an H or lose one from left to right? Bases Accept, Acids Donate.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: (a) Add one H<sup>+</sup> to Cl<sup>−</sup>. (b) Add one H<sup>+</sup> for the conjugate acid and remove one for the conjugate base, changing the charge by 1 each time.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Check the green-sheet strong lists first. Then ask: H written first (acid)? Metal hydroxide or amine (base)? Metal with another anion (salt)? None of these (neither)?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: The acid gives one H<sup>+</sup> to water to make H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. Is lactic acid on the six-acid strong list? That decides single or double arrow.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Ca<sup>2+</sup> pairs with two ClO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, so count the HClO<sub>4</sub> and waters needed. Name the salt: cation first, then the polyatomic anion from the green sheet.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Look for the functional group: –COOH means acid, an amine nitrogen (–NH<sub>2</sub>) means base, and an ester (–COO– between carbons) has neither.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Write each ion's conjugate acid (add H<sup>+</sup>) and check the strong-acid list. The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use K<sub>w</sub>: divide 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> by [OH<sup>−</sup>]. Then compare [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] with 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: NaOH is a strong base with one OH<sup>−</sup>, so [OH<sup>−</sup>] equals its molarity. Then divide K<sub>w</sub> by [OH<sup>−</sup>].

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Compare each given concentration with 10<sup>−7</sup> M (write out the zeros if it helps). For [OH<sup>−</sup>] in A, divide K<sub>w</sub> by A's [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>].

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Move the decimal point left as many places as the exponent says. Then line [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] up against neutral's 0.0000001 M.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: HCl is strong, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] equals its molarity. Take −log, and give as many decimal places as the concentration has significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: KOH is strong with one OH<sup>−</sup>: take −log[OH<sup>−</sup>] for the pOH, then use pH + pOH = 14.00.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Undo the log with the 10<sup>x</sup> key: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup>. Two decimal places in the pH give two significant figures. Then compare the pH with 7.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Compare the pH with the normal range, 7.35–7.45. Then use [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup> with the 10<sup>x</sup> key.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]; three significant figures give three decimal places. Then compare the pH with 7.35–7.45.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Map it out: g → mol NaOH → mol OH<sup>−</sup> → [OH<sup>−</sup>] (divide by liters) → pOH → pH.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Ask the two buffer questions: is there a weak acid (or weak base)? Is its conjugate partner, the same formula with one H<sup>+</sup> more or less, also there?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Each partner handles one threat: which one can accept a proton from H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, and which can donate one to OH<sup>−</sup>? Each product is the other partner plus water.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Rapid breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Follow CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> → H<sup>+</sup> + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>: less CO<sub>2</sub> means what for H<sup>+</sup>, and for pH?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Use process of elimination: cross out any pair with a strong acid, then any pair with no weak acid, then any pair whose members don't differ by one H<sup>+</sup>.

title: Problem 12.1
hint: For each choice, name the indicator and recall its color in acid and in base (BRA for litmus). Which kind of solution makes chalk fizz?

title: Problem 12.2
hint: (a) Match each color to the red cabbage chart in 12.1. (b) Lower pH is more acidic; look for two samples with the same color. (c) Bases turn red litmus blue. (d) Acid + bicarbonate makes which gas?

title: Problem 12.3
hint: (a) Acid + active metal → salt + hydrogen gas; aluminum forms Al<sup>3+</sup>. (b) Think about the gas and the metal. (c) Compare with the list of acid properties in 12.1.

title: Problem 12.4
hint: Swap partners first: what forms from H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>? Then use the unstable-products table to see what that product becomes.

title: Problem 12.5
hint: The salt is the base's cation with the acid's anion; Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> has two OH<sup>−</sup>, so it needs two acid molecules. For (c), cross out the spectator ions.

title: Problem 12.6
hint: Classify each pH first: below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Then check each indicator statement: BRA for litmus, pink above about pH 8 for phenolphthalein.

title: Problem 12.7
hint: (a) Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO<sub>2</sub>. (b) Does CaSO<sub>4</sub> contain a carbonate or bicarbonate? (c) Balance S first, then H with water, and O last.

title: Problem 12.8
hint: Brønsted–Lowry definitions are about a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) moving between substances. Recall what an acid does with the proton; a base does the opposite. Which choice is the older Arrhenius definition?

title: Problem 12.9
hint: For each reaction, follow the H<sup>+</sup>: the reactant that loses an H is the acid, and the one that gains it is the base. Each conjugate shares a common piece with its partner.

title: Problem 12.10
hint: A conjugate base has exactly one fewer H and a charge one lower than its acid.

title: Problem 12.11
hint: Conjugate base: remove one H<sup>+</sup> (one fewer H, charge down 1). Conjugate acid: add one H<sup>+</sup> (one more H, charge up 1). Watch the charges on the ions.

title: Problem 12.12
hint: A conjugate pair has one member on each side of the arrow, and the two differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup>.

title: Problem 12.13
hint: (a) As an acid, H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> gives one H<sup>+</sup> to OH<sup>−</sup>. (b) As a base, it takes one from H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. Check the charges. (c) See water's double role in 12.2.

title: Problem 12.14
hint: (a) Count C, H, N, and O on each side. (b) BAD: who donates the proton, and who accepts it? (c) Use the urea-to-NH<sub>3</sub> mole ratio; each NH<sub>3</sub> accepts one proton.

title: Problem 12.15
hint: Check the green-sheet strong lists first. Then: H first (acid), metal hydroxide or amine (base), metal with another anion (salt). Carbonates and bicarbonates can be salts and bases.

title: Problem 12.16
hint: Only six common acids are strong; recall the green-sheet list. Having more H atoms, or a halogen, does not make an acid strong.

title: Problem 12.17
hint: Is lactic acid on the green-sheet strong-acid list? How much of a weak acid ionizes, compared with a strong acid?

title: Problem 12.18
hint: Strong acids and bases get a single arrow; weak ones get a double arrow. Acids and amines react with water; hydroxides just dissociate (count the OH<sup>−</sup>).

title: Problem 12.19
hint: Most of the HX is still intact molecules. Is that a strong or a weak acid? Then find the choice that is not on the strong list.

title: Problem 12.20
hint: Salt = base's cation + acid's anion; balance so every H<sup>+</sup> meets an OH<sup>−</sup>. Check solubility on the green sheet. The number of waters equals the H<sup>+</sup> neutralized.

title: Problem 12.21
hint: Classify each substance as strong or weak first: strong gets a single arrow, weak a double arrow. Then check that each equation balances.

title: Problem 12.22
hint: Bulb brightness tracks how many ions are present. Which is a strong acid (all ions), which is weak (mostly molecules), and which forms no ions?

title: Problem 12.23
hint: (a) Check the green-sheet lists, then look for an amine, a carbonate, or an alcohol. (b)(c) Weak species get double arrows. (d) Strong acid + strong base: think about the heat released.

title: Problem 12.24
hint: Write water's autoionization: each H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> forms with one OH<sup>−</sup>. The two equal concentrations multiply to give K<sub>w</sub>; what must each one be?

title: Problem 12.25
hint: Divide K<sub>w</sub> by [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]. Then check: an acidic juice must have [OH<sup>−</sup>] below 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Problem 12.26
hint: Rearrange K<sub>w</sub> to find [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] from [OH<sup>−</sup>], then compare it with 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Problem 12.27
hint: Compare each value with 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M, and note whether it is [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] or [OH<sup>−</sup>]. Basic means [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] below 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Problem 12.28
hint: HBr is a strong acid, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] equals its molarity. Then divide K<sub>w</sub> by [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>].

title: Problem 12.29
hint: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> releases two OH<sup>−</sup> per formula unit, so find [OH<sup>−</sup>] first. Then divide K<sub>w</sub> by it; the question asks for H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

title: Problem 12.30
hint: Put every solution on the same scale: convert each [OH<sup>−</sup>] to [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] with K<sub>w</sub>, then rank from the largest [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] (most acidic) down.

title: Problem 12.31
hint: (a) Divide K<sub>w</sub> by [OH<sup>−</sup>] and compare with 10<sup>−7</sup> M. (b) Divide the two [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] values. (c) Is bicarbonate an acid or a base?

title: Problem 12.32
hint: Does K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] change when a base dissolves at 25 °C? If [OH<sup>−</sup>] goes up, what must happen to keep the product fixed?

title: Problem 12.33
hint: HNO<sub>3</sub> is strong, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] equals its molarity. Take −log, and count significant figures in the concentration for the decimal places.

title: Problem 12.34
hint: KOH is strong with one OH<sup>−</sup>. Take −log[OH<sup>−</sup>] for the pOH, then subtract from 14.00; two significant figures give two decimal places.

title: Problem 12.35
hint: Each Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives two OH<sup>−</sup>. Find [OH<sup>−</sup>], take −log for the pOH, subtract from 14.00, and watch the decimal places.

title: Problem 12.36
hint: Undo the pH with the 10<sup>x</sup> key: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup>. Two decimal places in the pH give two significant figures.

title: Problem 12.37
hint: Each row has one known value. Use the loop in 12.5: −log, 10<sup>x</sup>, K<sub>w</sub>, and pH + pOH = 14.00. In (d), the given value is the pOH.

title: Problem 12.38
hint: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]. Find the pH difference, then raise 10 to that power.

title: Problem 12.39
hint: (a) Use 10<sup>−pH</sup>; two decimal places give two significant figures. (b) Divide the two concentrations. (c) Compare with the normal range, 7.35–7.45.

title: Problem 12.40
hint: Count the significant figures in 4.80 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (does the trailing zero count?). That is the number of decimal places the pH gets.

title: Problem 12.41
hint: (a)(b) Use 10<sup>−pH</sup>; one decimal place in the pH means one significant figure. (c) Raise 10 to the pH difference. (d) Is carbonate an acid or a base?

title: Problem 12.42
hint: HCl is strong, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] equals its molarity. Take −log, then subtract from 14.00 for the pOH; count the significant figures in 0.080 carefully.

title: Problem 12.43
hint: Is lactic acid strong or weak? Compare the [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] it makes with that of 0.010 M HCl, then decide which way the pH moves.

title: Problem 12.44
hint: A buffer needs a weak acid with its own conjugate base (the same formula, one H<sup>+</sup> less). Cross out strong acids first, then check each partner.

title: Problem 12.45
hint: (a) Which species has the acidic H, and which is the same formula minus one H<sup>+</sup>? (b) The base partner takes H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. (c) The acid partner gives a proton to OH<sup>−</sup>. Leave Na<sup>+</sup> out.

title: Problem 12.46
hint: Added OH<sup>−</sup> needs something that can donate a proton to it. Which species in the blood buffer is the acid partner, and which is the base partner?

title: Problem 12.47
hint: (a) Follow the arrows: more CO<sub>2</sub> pushes toward more H<sup>+</sup>. (b) Compare 7.30 with 7.35–7.45 and ask what caused it. (c) Lungs vs. kidneys. (d) Compare blood with its normal range, not with 7.

title: Problem 12.48
hint: (a) Added acid reacts with the base partner, 1 : 1. (b) Subtract from one partner and add to the other. (c) What happens to the extra acid once the base partner runs out?

title: Problem 12.49
hint: A buffer needs a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Which part neutralizes added acid, and which neutralizes added base? Test HCl and Cl<sup>−</sup> against those two jobs.

title: Problem 12.50
hint: (a) Lactic acid donates its H<sup>+</sup> to HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. (b) H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> breaks down as in acid + carbonate reactions. (c) Where does the extra CO<sub>2</sub> go?

title: Problem 12.51
hint: (a) Use M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> (Section 11.4). (b) HCl is strong; take −log and count significant figures. (c) Use the red cabbage chart. (d) Take −log of the stock molarity.

title: Problem 12.52
hint: (a) Moles = L × M for each; they react 1 : 1, so subtract. (b) Divide the leftover moles by the total volume. (c) Leftover OH<sup>−</sup> means pOH first. (d) Phenolphthalein is pink above about pH 8.

title: Problem 12.53
hint: (a) The goal is the mole: g → mol antacid → mol HCl (from each equation) → volume of 0.0800 M acid. (c) Which product is a gas? (d) Check the green-sheet strong-base list.

title: Problem 12.54
hint: (a) Remove one H<sup>+</sup> from benzoic acid; add one H<sup>+</sup> to pyridine. (b) Look for a weak acid or weak base with its conjugate partner; ignore Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>. (c) Is HBr strong?

title: Problem 12.55
hint: (a) Grams → moles, then divide by liters. (b) KOH is strong with one OH<sup>−</sup>: pOH, then pH, then K<sub>w</sub>. (c) Use the cabbage chart. (d) Count the OH<sup>−</sup> per formula unit.

title: Problem 12.56
hint: A conjugate base is one rung down the proton ladder: one fewer H, and the charge goes down by 1.

title: Problem 12.57
hint: (a) Follow the H<sup>+</sup> from left to right (BAD). (b) Find the piece each pair shares. (c) Read right to left: does the conjugate acid hand its H<sup>+</sup> back to the conjugate base?

title: Problem 12.58
hint: Use [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup> with the 10<sup>x</sup> key. A high pH must mean a very small [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>].

title: Problem 12.59
hint: Map it out: g → mol Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> → mol OH<sup>−</sup> (two per formula unit) → [OH<sup>−</sup>] in mol/L → pOH → pH.

title: Problem 12.60
hint: (a) Balance first (Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> has two OH), then start from the side with both V and M: mL → mol Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> → mol HCl → mL. (b) [OH<sup>−</sup>] is twice the molarity.

title: Problem 12.61
hint: Cross out any pair with a strong acid. Then check that the two species differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup> and that both partners are present.

title: Problem 12.62
hint: Name the functional group in each compound. Which of those groups did Chapter 12 call acidic, which basic, and which neither?

title: Problem 12.63
hint: (a) Find which two powers of 10 the concentration sits between. (b) Take −log; two significant figures give two decimal places. (c) Compare with pH 7.
